svg.aria-label: Diagram: symmetric region pairs, asymmetric pairs where pairing runs one way only, and nonpaired regions that use availability zones instead, with what pairing does and does not provide
svg.title: Region pairs: symmetric, asymmetric, and none at all
svg.text: Pairing is an association, not a mechanism
It changes how Microsoft sequences updates and prioritises recovery. It does not move your workload anywhere.
Symmetric — most pairs
UK South ↔ UK West
Japan East ↔ Japan West
Each names the other. Almost all sit
inside the same geography, which is
what keeps data residency intact.
Asymmetric — not mutual
Brazil South → S Central US
S Central US → N Central US
Brazil South points at a region that
does not point back, in a different
geography. Check, do not assume.
Nonpaired — and growing
Italy North, Spain Central,
Poland Central, Qatar Central,
Mexico Central, and more
Many newer regions have no pair and
use availability zones instead.
What pairing actually gives you — three things, none of them failover
Recovery sequence: in a geography-wide outage, one region of each pair is prioritised for recovery.
Sequential updating: Azure strives to stagger planned system updates so a faulty update cannot hit both at once.
Data residency: almost all pairs sit within one geography, so replicating to the pair stays inside the boundary.
Only a small number of Azure services use pairs at all, and many support geo-redundancy between any two regions.
What it does not give you
Deploying into a paired region does not make resources more resilient, and provides no automatic high availability,
no disaster recovery capability and no failover. The plan is yours to write whether the region is paired or not.
Even where a service uses the pair, Microsoft-managed failover is not a primary DR strategy: for geo-redundant
storage it happens only in catastrophic situations, and only after repeated failed recovery attempts.
